title: The thirteenth of April

cards: How do you keep a festival and a funeral on the same day? In Amritsar, that isn't a riddle. It's the calendar.
In the morning, the city fills for Vaisakhi: the harvest is in, the Khalsa's birthday is sung, there's langar and color and noise.
And a short walk from the Harmandir Sahib there's a walled garden where, on a Vaisakhi long ago, troops fired into an unarmed crowd. People come to that garden on the same day, quietly.

teach.b: This path has told the story of Jallianwala Bagh, and the long memory of Udham Singh. Today is about what the date now carries.

The firing happened on Vaisakhi day, so ever since, Vaisakhi in Punjab has held a second memory inside the first. Some celebrate in the morning and remember in the afternoon, and the two sit side by side.
The crowd in the garden was Sikh, Hindu and Muslim together, some of them visitors in town for the festival.
So the memory doesn't belong to one community, and people of different faiths come to the garden to remember. The garden is a memorial now.
Visitors see the marks in the walls and the well, and some lower their voices without being told. A place can teach silence on its own. A line in the Guru Granth Sahib fits a mixed crowd.
On Ang 1299, Guru Arjan sings, in paraphrase, that no one is my enemy and no one is a stranger; I get along with all.
Some Sikhs hold that line beside the garden, because the people who died there were strangers to each other and are remembered together.
It's also a guard against the easy road from grief to hatred: remembering the garden doesn't mean making enemies of anyone living today.
So the festival isn't spoiled by the memory, and the memory isn't drowned by the festival.

how: On Vaisakhi, people visit the Jallianwala Bagh memorial in Amritsar to remember those killed there, while the city also celebrates the harvest and the birth of the Khalsa. Some gurdwaras include the memory of the garden in their Vaisakhi gatherings.

games.q: it's Vaisakhi in Amritsar. you've been to the Harmandir Sahib and eaten langar. what do people do with the afternoon?
o: visit the garden quietly to remember.
games.why: they keep both: the festival and the garden. the date holds two memories at once.

practice: Sit, or stand if you'd rather, and for one minute say nothing and do nothing, no phone, no plans, letting the silence be for the people in the garden, Sikh, Hindu and Muslim, visitors and neighbors, who came for a festival.
There's no need to picture what happened; when the minute feels done, breathe slowly and rest in the quiet a little longer. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them.

wordCard.voice: Jallianwala Bagh. The walled garden in Amritsar where an unarmed crowd of several faiths was fired on, a memory the thirteenth of April, Vaisakhi, also holds. Today's word.
